messages.subject: Trouble finding a suitable model
messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

I am currently analysing movement data of bats and this is the best selected model via ctmm.select() for a singular night.
As you can all see, there is a peak in my data, followed by a plunge, when the bat is returning to its roost. This peak is not acknowledged in the model whatsoever, creating a high percentage of my data, which is not explained by the model.

I, for sure, also know, that this is not an artifact, as the bat shows a similar pattern for the other nights it was observed.

Any ideas on how I can fit a better model?
Or is CTMM not capable of fitting a suitable one to my data?

Thank you in advance!

Janine

messages.subject: Re: Calibration Data for Error Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Christen,
I conducted a small calibration data collection for my gps collars. I stationed 3 collars in an open field location and 3 collars in an hedgerow adjacent location. Each collar collected 72 fixes in total over two days.
I looked at model selection values for individual collars in both habitats and thankfully, the individual error models had very similar results to joint models.
I then compared joint habitat model selection values with individual habitat model selection values and this was the result I got:

Vertical values are very similar, however there is a moderate difference between the horizontal AICc values. The difference in reduced z-squared value is relatively small. In your vignette for error data, you caution against selecting based on AICc values, if differences are somewhat similar. Do you think these differences necessitate a larger collection of gps in both habitats ?

Thanks for your help,
Aaron

messages.subject: Re: Trouble finding a suitable model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Janine,

That fit actually looks very good. The latter half of the variogram is very noisy, which is why it isn't plotted by default. You can improve the CIs on the empirical variogram with CI="Gauss" if the data are not too irregularly sampled. I assume the point estimates for the theoretical and empirical variograms will still be inside each other's CIs where the empirical variogram is reliable. That's what I would consider to be a very good fit. Substantial white space where the CIs don't overlap is what I would consider to be a bad fit.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: rsf.fit() mean() error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I'm currently working on this as well. I have been  running RSFs for each individual on a loop using rsf.select(), which has worked well overall (also I incorporated feedback from a previous post I made and you responded to - thank you!).

I'm wondering about selection bias when calculating mean() using rsf.select(), since not all individuals retained the same covariates in their top models. One source I looked at suggested removing the individuals from the mean calculation that did not retain the particular covariate that I'm calculating for. A different source warned of selection bias when doing this, and said to use rsf.fit() rather than rsf.select() so that all covariates are retained in the model for each individual (I get the idea behind it, but it makes me nervous).

I've tried several workarounds to try and bypass the error message that OP reported when using rsf.fit(), but no luck.

What are your thoughts on this? Also, I hope I'm correct in calculating means separately for each covariate (?).

Thanks!
Laura (UF PhD)

> Hi Laura,
>
> If you omit some categories, then your reference function is effectively the combined category of omitted categories.
>
> The reference category should not be rare. By default in ctmm, the reference category is taken to be the most common category. If the reference category has no data in it (or nearby available area for an RSF) then that's the same as not having a reference category at all.
>
> Categorical data are necessarily collinear if you try to use every category as an independent covariate, because they are dependent. If you are in one category then you can't be in any other category. The same thing happens if you choose a bad reference category with no data in it.
>
> For an RSF, it's not the raw amount of data but how many home-range crossings there are in that 12 months. What is the home-range crossing timescale, tau[position]?
>
> Another thing that can cause insignificant coefficients is having too many categories for the amount of data. Sometimes categories need to be meaningfully grouped together to get significant results.
>
> Since the ctmm models are currently stationary, you might consider subsetting the diurnal/nocturnal data to the day/night when the individuals are performing selection and not sitting in the same spot.
>
> Best,
> Chris

> > > > > We advise always using rsf.select() because we have found that poorly estimated coefficients can cause problems when estimating population-level averages. This often happens, for example, when a specific cover type is not in an animal's home range, or occurs very rarely. No need for a secondary rsf.fit() command.
> > > > >
> > > > > When using cover type data, remember that the coefficients are in comparison to a reference category (i.e., whatever cover type(s) is/are left out). A positive number is not selection for that coefficient--it is selection compared to the baseline reference category. I generally advise that folks make sure their reference category is relatively large (i.e., contains > 25% or so of an animal's locations, which ensures that selection for the reference category is well-estimated) and is visited roughly in proportion to availability (i.e., the proportion of locations in that cover type is roughly equal to the proportion that occurs in the home range or study area, which makes selection coefficients a little easier to interpret). I usually include very rare cover types (<2% of the landscape) in the reference category unless there is a priori reason to think they are biologically important, if exploratory analysis indicates that the animals really seem to seek them out, or if I am working with very large numbers of locations per animal that ensure that I have enough statistical power to detect biologically meaningful patterns of selection.

messages.subject: Re: rsf.fit() mean() error
messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura,

The dropped covariates are not supported by AIC and so they have extremely wide CIs and would not substantially contribute to the population model, even if computed exactly. In fact, their extremely wide CIs are the reason that they have to be dropped from the meta analysis, because their log-likelihood curvatures are too close to 1/Inf.

I don't know that I would ever calculate the covariate mean parameters separately. I can't see a reason for not using the best model.

Best,
Chris
